article_title: The Effects of the Elevate Math Summer Program on Math Achievement and Algebra Readiness
citation: Snipes, J., Huang, C.-W., Jaquet, K., & Finkelstein, N. (2016). The effects of the Elevate Math summer program on math achievement and algebra readiness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org/
title: MDTP Algebra Readiness test
description: The Mathematics Diagnostic Testing Project (MDTP) Algebra Readiness test was used to measure math achievement and define algebra readiness in the study. It "consists of 45 multiple-choice items in seven topic areas" and was administered on the first and last days of participation. Previous research cited by the authors found it highly predictive of success in grade 8 algebra I, with passing three or more topic areas indicating a greater than 50 percent chance of algebra success.
requirements: Administration to students at defined points in the program (first and last days)
target_learners: rising grade 8 students
target_learning_goals: algebra readiness assessment
examples: Used in this study to define math achievement (total score) and algebra readiness (three or more topic areas passed)
key_sources: Snipes, J., Huang, C.-W., Jaquet, K., & Finkelstein, N. (2016). The effects of the Elevate Math summer program on math achievement and algebra readiness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567052

article_title: Using Assessment Data to Guide Math Course Placement of California Middle School Students
citation: Chun-Wei Huang, Jason Snipes, Neal Finkelstein, WestEd. (2016). Using assessment data to guide math course placement of California middle school students. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Mathematics Diagnostic Testing Project (MDTP) grade 7 assessments
description: The MDTP is a diagnostic assessment of grade 7 students’ math performance and possibly algebra readiness that some SVRA districts began using in 2010 to assist algebra I placement decisions. The article describes that "The MDTP tests can be administered online, and the results are available immediately after completion," in contrast to CST results, which are not available until August or later. Three types of results are available: the number of MDTP topics mastered, the level of mastery of each topic, and the topic scores.
requirements: Online administration to produce immediately available results
target_learners: Grade 7 students being assessed for grade 8 algebra I placement
target_learning_goals: Diagnosing mathematics topic mastery and algebra readiness for course placement
examples: Some SVRA districts began using MDTP tests in 2010 to assist with initial algebra I placement decisions before grade 7 CST results become available
key_sources: Chun-Wei Huang, Jason Snipes, Neal Finkelstein, WestEd. (2016). Using assessment data to guide math course placement of California middle school students. SREE Spring 2016 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED567123

article_title: Hypergamigication Through Integrating Game Engines and Learning Management Systems: Ender's Game
citation: Araz Yusubov, Tangiz Alizada, Michael Bechtel. (2026). Hypergamigication Through Integrating Game Engines and Learning Management Systems: Ender's Game. https://github.com/ADA-SITE-SITE4890-2023-Spring/senior-design-project-ay5-gamification-2-0-unity-bb/
title: Parallels between MDA game components and learning materials, process, and outcomes
description: The paper maps the MDA model's mechanics, dynamics, and aesthetics onto learning materials, learning process, and learning outcomes, aligning game design with educational frameworks such as 3P and constructive alignment. It notes that "similar to how the MDA components are “causally linked,” the learning materials , process, and outcomes are mutually interlinked". This mapping grounds the design of LMS-game integration, where game objects correspond to course objects.
requirements: A course whose materials, process, and outcomes can be identified and matched to game mechanics, dynamics, and aesthetics
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: aligning game experiences with course learning outcomes
examples: Figure 1 pairs Game Designer/Instructional Designer, Mechanics/Learning Materials, Dynamics/Learning Process, Aesthetics/Learning Outcomes, and Player/Learner
key_sources: Araz Yusubov, Tangiz Alizada, Michael Bechtel. (2026). Hypergamigication Through Integrating Game Engines and Learning Management Systems: Ender's Game. https://github.com/ADA-SITE-SITE4890-2023-Spring/senior-design-project-ay5-gamification-2-0-unity-bb/

article_title: Effects of Fact Retrieval Tutoring on Third‐Grade Students with Math Difficulties with and without Reading Difficulties
citation: Powell, S. R., Fuchs, L. S., Fuchs, D., Cirino, P. T., & Fletcher, J. M. (2009). Effects of Fact Retrieval Tutoring on Third-Grade Students with Math Difficulties with and without Reading Difficulties. Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 24(1), 1-11. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.01272.x
title: MD subtype framework: MD-only versus MDRD differential difficulty
description: The article evaluates Geary's hypothesis that math difficulty subtypes represent distinct cognitive profiles. MDRD students' concurrent math and reading difficulty is attributed to weak phonological processing that hinders acquisition of vocabulary and math facts, whereas MD-only students' poor fact recall is attributed to weak number sense. The randomized trial's differential responsiveness finding is offered as support that MD-only versus MDRD "may represent a viable scheme for subtyping mathematics disability."
requirements: Subtype classification via math and reading screening cutoffs (WRAT Arithmetic and Reading percentiles)
constraints: The study was not designed to determine whether response differences are due to phonological processing or number sense skills
target_learners: Third-grade students with math difficulties
target_learning_goals: Automatic retrieval of basic number combinations
examples: Students were classified as MD-only (WRAT Arithmetic <26th percentile, WRAT Reading >39th percentile) or MDRD (Arithmetic <26th and Reading <25th percentile) and randomized within subtype.

Effects of Fact Retrieval Tutoring on Third-Grade Students with Math Difficulties with and without Reading Difficulties. article_title: Performance and acceptance when using tablets as a multiple document learning tool: do application and guidance matter?
citation: Jordan Lombard, Ivar Bråten, Cécile van de Leemput, Franck Amadieu. (2021). Performance and acceptance when using tablets as a multiple document learning tool: do application and guidance matter? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09537-6
title: MD-TRACE model of task-based multiple document processing
description: The article describes the Multiple-Document Task-based Relevance Assessment and Content Extraction model by Rouet and Britt (2011) as "a prominent framework describing the steps in working with multiple documents to complete a particular task". It consists of five steps: interpreting the task instruction and setting goals, judging which external resources are needed, selecting and processing documents, creating a task product, and evaluating its alignment with task requirements, with a cyclical return to earlier steps. The study particularly targeted the third and fourth steps: strategy guidance addressed step-three processes and effects were assessed through written task products in step four.
requirements: Working through the model's steps draws on external resources, such as a task instruction and a document set, and internal resources, such as prior knowledge and reading skills
constraints: The article applies the model to a single-issue document set on a controversial socio-scientific issue and evaluates only steps three and four empirically
target_learners: undergraduate students working with multiple documents
target_learning_goals: multiple document comprehension and integration of information across documents
examples: All participants received a task instruction, an iPad Pro, and five documents on sun exposure and health, framing the task in MD-TRACE terms
key_sources: Jordan Lombard, Ivar Bråten, Cécile van de Leemput, Franck Amadieu. (2021). Performance and acceptance when using tablets as a multiple document learning tool: do application and guidance matter? Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-021-09537-6

article_title: The Landscape of Research on Prior Knowledge and Learning: a Bibliometric Analysis
citation: Bittermann, A., McNamara, D., Simonsmeier, B. A., & Schneider, M. (2023). The Landscape of Research on Prior Knowledge and Learning: a Bibliometric Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09775-9
title: Multidimensional Knowledge in Text Comprehension (MDK-C) framework
description: The MDK-C framework describes how four dimensions of prior knowledge — amount, accuracy, specificity, and coherence — determine learners' understanding of texts. It assumes prior content knowledge is represented as a multidimensional mental model or semantic network in which spreading activation makes semantically related and interconnected knowledge more likely, and faster, to be activated. The article presents it as a recent development aimed at enabling more nuanced predictions about knowledge use during comprehension.
requirements: Clearer definitions and boundaries around the dimensions of prior knowledge, which the article states is the framework's underlying motivation
constraints: The framework concerns text and discourse comprehension specifically, not learning in general
target_learners: readers of texts and discourse, including students in comprehension research
target_learning_goals: text and discourse comprehension supported by prior knowledge
examples: The article cites the framework (McCarthy & McNamara, 2021) as an example of recent work distinguishing amount, accuracy, specificity, and coherence of prior knowledge
key_sources: Bittermann, A., McNamara, D., Simonsmeier, B. A., & Schneider, M. (2023). The Landscape of Research on Prior Knowledge and Learning: a Bibliometric Analysis. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09775-9

article_title: Physiological synchrony amongst medical residents during crisis management simulation training and a video-based assessment of leaders’ performance
citation: Lucia Patino Melo, Sebastian Wallot, Keerat Grewal, Matthew Moreno, Osamu Nomura, Jason M. Harley. (2026). Physiological synchrony amongst medical residents during crisis management simulation training and a video-based assessment of leaders' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102302
title: MdRQA %REC with surrogate-data comparison for detecting group physiological synchrony
description: Multidimensional Recurrence Quantification Analysis (MdRQA) is the analytic method the article uses to quantify physiological synchrony in multivariate EDA time series. It extends cross-recurrence analysis and "can handle multivariate time series data... and is not limited to bi-variate analyses". The study focused on the %REC output, the proportion of recurrent points in phase space, and validated detected synchrony by comparing real teams' %REC against surrogate datasets created by randomizing each participant's z-scored EDA values within a group. Radius was tuned so %REC ranged from 5 to 20% for comparability across datasets.
requirements: Time-delayed embedding parameters (emb: 1, del = 21, rad = 0.2, Euclidean norm) and radius tuning to keep %REC between 5 and 20% for comparability
constraints: Surrogate datasets with non-group members were not feasible due to differing recording lengths and sample size limitations; no in situ movement-artifact controls were used, with artifacts addressed post hoc via visual inspection and filtering
target_learners: medical trainees in team-based simulation education
target_learning_goals: detecting shared emotional arousal in collaborative learning teams
examples: Applied to EDA from 29 residents in 9 teams wearing Empatica E4 wristbands before and during CRM scenarios
key_sources: Lucia Patino Melo, Sebastian Wallot, Keerat Grewal, Matthew Moreno, Osamu Nomura, Jason M. Harley. (2026). Physiological synchrony amongst medical residents during crisis management simulation training and a video-based assessment of leaders' performance. Learning and Instruction 102 (2026) 102302. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102302

article_title: A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills
citation: Potocki, A., Ayroles, J., & Rouet, J.-F. (2023). A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101781. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101781
title: MD-TRACE model of purposeful reading
description: MD-TRACE (Rouet & Britt, 2011) describes purposeful reading as a cyclical sequence of steps: the reader builds a task model from the instruction, searches for relevant information, selectively processes and integrates it into a task product, and checks the product against the question's requirements, recycling if needed. The article highlights "the role of goal formation and monitoring, and the cyclical nature of the activity, with several recycling loops corresponding to metacognitive processes". The training program's five modules were mapped onto the model's four steps plus an integrative module.
requirements: Readers must understand task instructions to build an appropriate task model, which the article identifies as key to reading outcomes
target_learners: elementary school students, especially 5th graders
target_learning_goals: purposeful reading: constructing task models, locating, extracting and integrating information, and evaluating answers
examples: The Purposeful Reading Training Program devoted its first four modules to Steps 1-4 of MD-TRACE and a final module to coordinating all steps
key_sources: Potocki, A., Ayroles, J., & Rouet, J.-F. (2023). A short teacher-led intervention using direct instruction enhances 5th graders' purposeful reading skills. Learning and Instruction, 86, 101781. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2023.101781

article_title: Psychological effects of gamified didactics with exergames in Physical Education at primary schools: Results from a natural experiment
citation: Quintas, A., Bustamante, J.-C., Pradas, F., & Castellar, C. (2020). Psychological effects of gamified didactics with exergames in Physical Education at primary schools: results from a natural experiment. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103874
title: Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics (MDA) framework adapted to educational gamification
description: The article uses the Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics framework (Hunicke et al., 2004) as its organising gamification model, adapted to the education field. It defines mechanics as "the system's set of constituent elements, the relation linking between them, and the way in which a system can routinely function", dynamics as how the player-student interacts with the mechanics, and aesthetics as the perceptions and sensations-emotions experienced by students while playing. The authors chose MDA over the Points-Badges-Leaderboards system because PBL "only fits one player type: 'achievers'", whereas MDA was used "to achieve an inclusive gamified atmosphere for all student-player types".
requirements: Design must attend to dynamic and aesthetic spheres in class, and not only to gamification mechanics such as the PBL system, per the authors' discussion.
constraints: The authors argue the PBL gamification system only fits one player type (achievers), which motivated the use of MDA instead.
target_learners: Primary school students (Year 6 and Year 7) in Physical Education classes
target_learning_goals: Motivation, dispositional flow, basic psychological needs, rhythmic motor skill, and commitment to learning in PE
examples: Mechanics used in the study included a system of positive points, rewards, classifications, levels of difficulty, challenges, achievements, badges, cooperative and competitive teams, virtual avatars, and avatar personalisation; aesthetics drew on the Just Dance Now exergame and the ClassDojo application.
key_sources: Quintas, A., Bustamante, J.-C., Pradas, F., & Castellar, C. (2020). Psychological effects of gamified didactics with exergames in Physical Education at primary schools: results from a natural experiment. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2020.103874

title: mDPBL multimedia learning for Computer Networks with routing animation
description: A multimedia learning package in a Direct Problem-Based Learning approach for Computer Networks, developed at Dian Nuswantoro University. It "includes the animation about Routing as a part of Computer Networks subject" and integrates "animation lessons, and other features with DPBL approach to supporting the student learning process". Students rated its usefulness, contents and navigation positively.

article_title: Effectiveness of an MDT-CDIO integrated teaching model in orthopedic clinical education: a controlled study.
citation: Nian Zhixuan, Li Mingchun, Liang Junwen, Li Yijia, Wei Ziting, Pan Liqiang, Fang Sen, Yang Xudong, Du Wenjia, Yun Xiangdong. (2026). Effectiveness of an MDT-CDIO integrated teaching model in orthopedic clinical education: a controlled study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09758-8
title: MDT-CDIO integrated teaching model: four-phase closed-loop clinical learning cycle with multidisciplinary role assignment
description: The article integrates the multidisciplinary team (MDT) model with the Conceive–Design–Implement–Operate (CDIO) framework, which "embodies the translation and adaptation of competency-based engineering education principles into the medical education context." Teaching proceeds through four phases: Conception (open-ended cases requiring differential diagnosis), Design (five-student groups with assigned clinical roles conducting a 30-minute simulated MDT consultation), Implementation (physician critique of student plans, bedside care, surgical participation, and an "MDT Full Process Log"), and Operation (patient follow-up and weekly debriefing sessions). The MDT component adds collaborative decision-making across orthopedics, radiology, rehabilitation, anesthesiology, and nursing to address the single-discipline limitations of CDIO alone.
requirements: A multidisciplinary teaching team of attending physicians and senior staff from orthopedics, radiology, rehabilitation, anesthesiology, nursing, and other relevant disciplines
A joint workshop before commencement to standardize instructional objectives and feedback mechanisms for each CDIO phase
A standardized clinical teaching database of open-ended cases
constraints: 18% of students reported difficulties integrating diverse expert perspectives during the initial training phase
12% of students suggested increasing hands-on clinical practice time to better apply theoretical knowledge
target_learners: orthopedic clinical internship students
medical students in clinical internship phase
target_learning_goals: orthopedic theoretical knowledge
clinical operational skills
interdisciplinary collaboration
clinical reasoning
communication and consensus-building
examples: Students in groups of five assumed roles of orthopedic surgeon, radiologist, physical therapist, specialist nurse, or anesthesiologist and conducted a 30-minute simulated MDT consultation for a full-thickness rotator cuff tear case with type 2 diabetes
key_sources: Nian Zhixuan, Li Mingchun, Liang Junwen, Li Yijia, Wei Ziting, Pan Liqiang, Fang Sen, Yang Xudong, Du Wenjia, Yun Xiangdong. (2026). Effectiveness of an MDT-CDIO integrated teaching model in orthopedic clinical education: a controlled study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09758-8

In the intervention, weekly sessions by an interdisciplinary team used case presentations, treatment planning exercises, and decision-making simulations to situate learning in authentic multidisciplinary contexts.

clinical reasoning
collaborative decision-making

article_title: Development and application of a multidimensional instrument to evaluate competency discrepancies in orthodontic practice.
citation: Cheung Chiyuen, Lu Hongfei, Tu Shaoqin, Chen Xinyuan, Feng Yi, Shao YiTing, Liu Yuyao, Mai Zhihui, Ai Hong, Chen Zheng. (2026). Development and application of a multidimensional instrument to evaluate competency discrepancies in orthodontic practice. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08237-2
title: Three-component multidisciplinary competency assessment instrument for orthodontists (SCS, CPBS, OKTO)
description: A three-component instrument assessing orthodontists' multidisciplinary competencies across dental, periodontal, TMJ, and myofunctional domains: the Subjective Competency Scale (12 items), the Clinical Practice Behavior Scale, and the Objective Knowledge Test for Orthodontists (19 questions). It was developed through a two-round expert review and scored with a weighted composite (MDT = 0.3×SCS + 0.4×CPBS + 0.3×OKTO) based on Miller's pyramid of clinical competence. The article reports the SCS showed "internal consistency of α = 0.897" and CFA confirmed its four-factor structure (CFI = 0.933), while the OKTO's KR-20 was 0.46, attributed to intentional multidomain heterogeneity.
requirements: Respondents must be practicing orthodontists with a minimum of six months of clinical experience
Attention-check questions verify basic orthodontic expertise before inclusion
constraints: Preliminary validation based on a Chinese sample; the article states it "requires further validation across diverse contexts"
The low OKTO KR-20 (0.46) introduces greater measurement error in the knowledge dimension
target_learners: Practicing orthodontists
Orthodontic residents and clinical fellows in standardized training programs
target_learning_goals: Multidisciplinary clinical competencies across dental, periodontal, TMJ, and myofunctional domains of orthodontic practice
examples: Administered online to 434 practicing Chinese orthodontists via the Wenjuanxing platform from January to June 2025
key_sources: Cheung Chiyuen, Lu Hongfei, Tu Shaoqin, Chen Xinyuan, Feng Yi, Shao YiTing, Liu Yuyao, Mai Zhihui, Ai Hong, Chen Zheng. (2026). article_title: Integrating multidisciplinary team teaching with case-based learning in urology internship education.
citation: Tang Shiying, Deng Shaohui, Tian Yu, Qiu Min, Zhang Shudong. (2026). Integrating multidisciplinary team teaching with case-based learning in urology internship education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08730-w
title: MDT-enhanced CBL: a case-based learning pattern in which a multidisciplinary specialist team jointly teaches real clinical cases
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern combining case-based learning with a multidisciplinary team of instructors. Students with foundational knowledge discuss real clinical cases to identify gaps in understanding, then a urology specialist leads instructors from radiology and ultrasonography to jointly teach the disease. The article states its "core emphasizes close interdisciplinary collaboration and knowledge complementarity, fostering a complete clinical reasoning process in students". In the study it was implemented in urology internship rotations with joint lesson planning and small-group sessions.
requirements: A convened MDT teaching team (lead urology attending, consultant radiologist, consultant ultrasonographer) participating in joint lesson planning and present during small-group sessions
Real clinical cases reviewed and standardized by the MDT team for the interns' learning level
Student preparatory self-study before the session
constraints: Evaluated only as a single approximately 4-hour session in a urology internship pilot with a convenience sample
target_learners: final-year clinical medicine interns in urology rotations
target_learning_goals: urological knowledge and clinical reasoning
image and ultrasound interpretation
interdisciplinary collaboration
examples: The experimental group's session integrated history taking and physical examination on actual patients, structured group discussion, and specialist-taught imaging content, over approximately 4 hours
key_sources: Tang Shiying, Deng Shaohui, Tian Yu, Qiu Min, Zhang Shudong. (2026). Integrating multidisciplinary team teaching with case-based learning in urology internship education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08730-w

article_title: The effects of video-based and blended learning on medication dosage calculation skills of paramedic students: A randomized, quasi-experimental study.
citation: Baran L, Öztürk H. (2025). The effects of video-based and blended learning on medication dosage calculation skills of paramedic students: A randomized, quasi-experimental study. Medicine 104(31):e43651. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000043651
title: Medication Dosage Calculation Skills Test (MDCST) with isomorphic parallel versions
description: The MDCST is a 20-question test adapted from Öztürk and Güneş (2023) assessing medication dosage calculation across five topics: "Units of Measure and Conversions," "Tablets and Capsules," "Oral Suspensions," "Injections" and "Infusion Treatments." It was reconstructed into 2 isomorphic versions by changing numerical values while preserving question structure, keeping difficulty consistent and reducing recall of original items. Each correct answer earned 5 points, scored out of 100.

constraints: Scores reflect written test performance, which the authors caution may not predict success in practical environments
target_learners: Emergency Medical Technician-Paramedic (EMTP) students
target_learning_goals: Medication dosage calculation skills, including unit conversions, tablets and capsules, oral suspensions, injections, and infusion treatments
examples: Used as pre-MDCST and post-MDCST around the 2-week intervention, with the isomorphic second version administered at posttest

article_title: Analysis of the applicability and utility of a gamified didactics with exergames at primary schools: Qualitative findings from a natural experiment.
citation: Quintas-Hijós Alejandro, Peñarrubia-Lozano Carlos, Bustamante Juan Carlos. (2020). Analysis of the applicability and utility of a gamified didactics with exergames at primary schools: Qualitative findings from a natural experiment. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0231269
title: The Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics (MDA) gamification architecture adapted to education for inclusive gamified atmospheres
description: The study used the Mechanics-Dynamics-Aesthetics (MDA) architecture, adapted to the education field, to achieve an inclusive gamified atmosphere for all student-player types, instead of the Points-Badges-Leaderboards architecture which fits only the "achiever" profile. Mechanics refers to the system's set of constituent elements and their relations; Dynamics refers to how mechanics effectively work adding the player factor; Aesthetics refers to perceptions and sensations-emotions experienced by students while playing. Design elements included positive points, rewards, classifications, levels of difficulty, challenges, achievements, badges, cooperative and competitive teams, and customizable virtual avatars, with no negative points of any kind.
requirements: Design elements specified in the study's Table 1, including a system of positive points, rewards, classifications, levels of difficulty, challenges, achievements, badges, cooperative and competitive teams, virtual avatars and avatar personalization
constraints: No negative points of any kind were used
